afflictions: early_blight; late_blight; blossom_end_rot; tomato_hornworm; aphids; corn_earworm
notes: Can be planted deep, up to the first true leaves; buried stem grows roots. Keeps fruiting until frost.
Sets most fruit at once; do not remove suckers. Good for containers and canning.
Needs warm nights; flowers drop below about 55 F or above 90 F.
Most heat-loving of the common nightshades; struggles in short, cool seasons.
Wind pollinated: plant in blocks of at least 4 rows, not one long row. Supersweet types need soil near 65 F.
Seeds rot in cold, wet soil. Pick often to keep pods coming.
Twines around poles or corn stalks; thin netting is a poor fit.
Stops producing once days are regularly above about 80 F. Tendrils need thin netting or string.
Hill soil over stems as they grow to keep tubers covered. Acid soil (below 6.0) reduces scab.
Pick at 6-8 in. Roots dislike disturbance; transplant only in peat or paper pots.
The 'mulch' of the Three Sisters. Cure in a warm, dry spot for 10-14 days before storing.
Spacing assumes a trellis; sprawling vines need about 36 in. Bitter fruit usually means water stress.
Seed needs light to germinate; barely cover. Seed goes dormant in soil above about 80 F. Tolerates shade in summer.
Bolts as days lengthen; in far-north summers, sow very early or in late summer for fall.
Frost sweetens the leaves. Harvest lower leaves first and leave the growing tip.
Heads split if heavy rain follows dry spells; water evenly.
Cut the main head before flowers open; side shoots follow for weeks.
Each 'seed' is a cluster; thin to one seedling per spot.
Keep the surface moist until seedlings emerge. Rocky or compacted soil forks roots.
Greens are edible. Seed clusters produce several seedlings; thin early.
Fastest crop in the garden; useful as a row marker sown with slow carrots.
Bulbing is set by day length: grow long-day types in the north (above about 37 N), short-day in the south. Stop watering when tops fall over.
Plant cloves in fall, about 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes; mulch over winter. Harvest when lower third of leaves brown.
Light harvest in year 2, full harvest from year 3; a bed can produce for 15-20 years. Leave summer ferns to feed the crowns.
Needs winter cold; thrives in Alaska. Leaves are toxic; eat stalks only. Remove flower stalks.
Blackens below about 50 F. Pinch flower buds to keep leaves coming.
Bolts fast in heat; seeds are coriander.
Slow to sprout; soak seed overnight. Host plant for swallowtail caterpillars. Flowers and dies in year 2.
Flowers attract beneficial wasps and hoverflies. Self-seeds freely.
Divide clumps every 3-4 years. Flowers are edible.
Spreads by runners and takes over beds; grow in a container or a sunken pot.
Wet winter soil kills it faster than cold. Surface sow; seed needs light.
Set the crown exactly at soil level. June-bearers fruit once; everbearers fruit in waves. Replant every 3-4 years.
Spreads by suckers; keep rows 12-18 in wide. Avoid sites where tomatoes or potatoes grew (verticillium wilt).
Fails in neutral soil: test pH before planting. Plant two varieties for better pollination. Half-high types suit zone 3.
Grown densely as a cover crop, roots suppress root-knot nematodes; a few scattered plants do much less.
Flowers best in lean soil; rich soil gives leaves, few blooms. Flowers and leaves are edible. Often used as an aphid trap crop.
Tolerates low light but variegation fades. Trails or climbs.
Overwatering is the usual cause of death; water every 2-6 weeks depending on light.
Leaf splits (fenestrations) need bright indirect light and a mature plant.
Droops visibly when thirsty and recovers within hours of watering.
Brown tips often come from fluoride or salts in tap water. Plantlets root easily.
